turns.prompt_text: My beekeeper friend has an entire trailer full of bee supers which are medium Hive boxes all filled with frames and good comb. He's had it there for 3 years because he used a product called Hot shot. He bought at Menards to try to deter pests from the hives which ended up killing like 15 of his hives. I think it was within 2 weeks. Some of them actually died because they couldn't get away but a lot of them just absconded I find it odd but I don't know much about Hot shot or how potent it is He was recommended to use Hot shot by the state apierist of Iowa so I imagine they just used it in a different way It sounds like like beekeeper friend just hung it nearby The hives and that's all it took
turns.response_html:
There was definitely a major miscommunication between what the state apiarist recommended and how your friend actually applied it.

The short answer is that the product is incredibly potent. It is a common and effective tool in beekeeping, but it is only meant for stored equipment—never for live, active colonies. Hanging it near active hives created a toxic vapor cloud that either killed the bees directly or forced the survivors to abscond.

What is Hot Shot?

"Hot Shot No-Pest Strips" are plastic strips infused with an organophosphate insecticide called Dichlorvos (DDVP).

Unlike sprays that settle on surfaces, DDVP works by continuously releasing a heavy, penetrating vapor into the air over the course of about four months. It is designed specifically to build up in enclosed, unventilated spaces (like garages or sheds) to kill flying and crawling insects. Because bees are insects, DDVP is highly lethal to them.

The State Apiarist's Advice (What Was Meant)

When apiarists in Iowa and other states recommend Hot Shot strips, they are recommending them exclusively to control wax moths and small hive beetles in stored supers during the off-season.

The correct, standard application in beekeeping looks like this:

  1. You stack all your empty supers with drawn comb for winter storage.
  2. You place one Hot Shot strip at the top of the stack.
  3. You seal the top and bottom of the stack to make it airtight.
  4. The heavy vapor sinks down through the frames, killing any wax moth larvae that try to destroy the drawn comb.
  5. Crucially: Before those supers ever touch a live hive again in the spring, the strip is removed, and the boxes are aired out in a cross-breeze for several days so the vapor completely dissipates.

The Fatal Error

By hanging the strip near the apiary, your friend essentially fumigated the immediate environment. Because the vapor constantly off-gasses, any foragers returning to the hives—or even the hives themselves if the wind blew the vapor into the entrances—were exposed to a heavy dose of neurotoxins.

When a hive is exposed to this kind of chemical stress, the bees that don't die outright will recognize the environment as hostile and immediately abscond to save the colony.

Are the trailer supers safe now?

Yes. If those medium supers and frames have been sitting in the trailer for three years, the drawn comb is entirely safe to use. DDVP is highly volatile, meaning it doesn't leave a permanent, sticky residue like some agricultural pesticides; it turns into gas and dissipates over time.

After three years, the chemical is long gone. As long as he airs the boxes out for a day or two to remove any stale trailer smell, those frames and that good comb can go right back into rotation.

turns.prompt_text: Interesting. So it sounds like it has kind of maybe a half-life system, but maybe not that exact system Like it loses potency rapidly. I mean at 3 days is enough He's very afraid of it because of how much it cost him, but knowing the truth helps out quite a bit here
turns.response_html:
It is completely understandable why your friend is terrified of those supers. Losing 15 hives is a massive financial and emotional blow—not just the cost of the bees themselves, but the lost time and honey production. Once you associate a piece of equipment with a wipeout like that, trusting it again is hard.

Your instinct about how it works is spot on, though the mechanism is less about a chemical "half-life" and more about volatility (off-gassing).

Here is exactly why that comb is safe to use now, and why just a few days of airing out is enough.

The "Perfume Effect" (Volatilization)

DDVP (the chemical in Hot Shot) has a very high vapor pressure. This means it desperately wants to turn from a solid/liquid state into a gas and mix with the air.

Think of it like a spilled bottle of strong perfume in a closet:

  • Closed space: If the closet doors are shut, the perfume vapor saturates the air and just hangs there. It remains incredibly potent because the gas has nowhere to go. This is how the strips protect stored boxes from wax moths.
  • Open space: If you open the closet doors, open a window, and turn on a fan, the wind physically picks up those gas molecules and carries them away. The smell (and the chemical) disappears rapidly.

Why 3 Days is Enough

When apiarists recommend airing out the boxes for a few days before spring use, they are relying on air currents to flush the remaining vapor out of the woodenware. Three days in a cross-breeze is enough to entirely replace the contaminated air inside the deeps and supers with fresh air.

Since your friend's trailer has presumably had some level of air exchange over the last three years—and the original vapor strip is long gone—that gas dissipated years ago.

The "Wax Sponge" Exception

The biggest fear with contaminated beekeeping equipment is usually the beeswax itself. Wax is a lipid (fat), which makes it act like a chemical sponge. Many agricultural pesticides and even in-hive mite treatments are lipophilic (fat-soluble), meaning they soak directly into the comb and permanently poison it.

DDVP is different. It does not bind well to wax or wood. It strictly wants to be a gas. Because it doesn't embed itself into the honeycomb, removing the air removes the poison.

Getting that drawn comb back into action will be a huge asset, saving his bees the massive energy cost of drawing new wax.
